paras: The Barbourville posse fight was a gunfight on the night of July 12, 1903, near Barbourville, Kentucky, between deputy sheriffs of Barbourville and a band of eight Black men from Clay county whom the deputies were pursuing. About twenty shots were fired and one of the men was dangerously wounded, while the rest escaped into Clay county. The only account is a short Associated Press dispatch, which ran in at least sixteen white papers across the country.

According to the dispatch, the eight men had tried to rob stores in the area; most copies say 'county stores', while the Portland and Savannah papers print 'country stores'. The accusation appears only as the dispatch states it, and no report names the stores, the men or the deputies.

The deputies set out after the band as a posse, and when overtaken the men 'gave resistance', in the dispatch's words. Twenty shots were fired in what the dispatch called 'a desperate fight', without saying who fired first or how many shots came from each side. One of the band was 'dangerously wounded', and the Berea Citizen's version adds that 'the balance of the band escaped to Clay county.'
No report of an arrest, of the wounded man's fate, or of any further pursuit into Clay county was found in the coverage.

The dispatch, datelined Barbourville, July 13, ran on July 14 in papers from Maine to Georgia, the Raleigh News & Observer crediting it to the Associated Press. Headlines framed it by race: the Indianapolis Journal used 'FIGHT WITH NEGROES', the Savannah Morning News 'NEGROES AND DEPUTIES / Engaged in a Desperate Running Fight', and the Portland Daily Press 'NEGROES AND SHERIFFS FIGHT'. The Louisville Courier-Journal headed it 'NEGROES FIGHT SHERIFFS / Flee Into Clay County After Firing Twenty Shots', attributing the shooting to the Black men, which the body text it printed does not do.

Kentucky's Berea Citizen carried a version datelined July 14 that placed the fight on 'Sunday night', and weeklies kept reprinting it, the Ohio Democrat as late as July 30. Condensed versions shed detail: the Springfield Weekly Republican set it in a roundup of racial clashes without naming Clay county, and the Owosso Times dropped the robbery charge altogether. No Black newspaper report of the episode was found.
Copies of the dispatch differ on whether the stores were 'county' or 'country' stores, and the Courier-Journal's headline alone has the Black men doing the firing.

reader.title: Barbourville posse fight (1903)
bases: Deputy sheriffs of Barbourville, acting as a posse, pursued a band of eight Black men accused of attempting to rob stores and exchanged twenty shots with them, dangerously wounding one (A1, A4, A12).

Every report is the same Associated Press dispatch from Barbourville (A10 credits the AP), so the papers agree only because they reprint one account, which comes from the officers' side (A1, A4, A12).

accounts.label: Wire report (Associated Press, Barbourville)
accounts.gist: Eight Clay county Black men tried to rob stores, resisted the deputies' posse that pursued them, and in the twenty-shot fight one was dangerously wounded before the rest escaped to Clay county. The account gives only the officers' version.

framing.detail: Papers ran the AP text unchanged under headlines such as 'FIGHT WITH NEGROES' (Indianapolis), 'NEGROES AND DEPUTIES / Engaged in a Desperate Running Fight' (Savannah) and 'NEGROES AND SHERIFFS FIGHT' (Portland), treating the robbery charge as fact.

The Louisville Courier-Journal headed it 'NEGROES FIGHT SHERIFFS / Flee Into Clay County After Firing Twenty Shots', assigning all the shooting to the Black men, though the dispatch says only that twenty shots were fired.
